speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is what this Bill seeks to do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Like our other laws, we regularly review the CDSA and CPC to ensure that they remain relevant and effective.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Money laundering, in particular, is one crime which has evolved significantly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Money launderers are finding new ways to evade detection, taking advantage of technological innovations meant to facilitate legitimate financial and business transactions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Consequently, international standards against money laundering have been enhanced.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This includes those set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international body that sets global standards to tackle money laundering and terrorism and proliferation financing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Each new money laundering case uncovered in Singapore or around the world provides useful lessons and this includes our $3 billion case.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have been distilling the learning points through careful studies of the changing modus operandi, as well as the new standards promulgated by FATF.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This Bill is a continuation of our ongoing efforts to ensure that Singapore’s regime keeps pace with evolving standards and trends, so that we can continue to deal effectively with attempts to launder criminal proceeds through Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These numbers are bigger than the gross domestic product (GDP) of most countries, Singapore included.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the ocean of money flows, criminal proceeds are like toxic waste that gets carried along.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Inevitably, some of them enter pristine waters, polluting rivers and estuaries, much against the wishes of local communities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Illicit monies flow through many jurisdictions, but are especially attracted to global financial centres, such as London, Hong Kong, New York, Delaware, Switzerland and Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is because the open, efficient and well-connected infrastructure of such centres that makes them attractive to legitimate investors is also useful for criminals to move and hide their monies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I shared some examples with Parliament last year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The authorities seized more than US$21 million worth of assets as part of the operation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In April, two managers of a Saudi oil exploration company went on trial in Switzerland for alleged fraud and money laundering of at least US$1.8 billion.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Singapore strives to be a reputable, trusted and thriving financial and business hub.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have a hard-earned track record and every intention to keep our system clean.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This must mean keeping money launderers out of our system as best as we can.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our anti-money laundering regime has three pillars: (a) prevention through a robust legal and regulatory framework to deter such criminals; (b) detection to ensure that illicit activities are picked up early; and (c) enforcement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We take firm and prompt enforcement action against money laundering.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this Bill, we have proposed enhancements across all three pillars to empower our agencies with strengthened levers and toolkits against money laundering.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, on our AML/CFT framework for casino operators.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Customer due diligence (CDD) checks conducted by gatekeepers in various sectors, is key to preventing suspicious individuals from sinking roots into our system and detecting any illicit activities early.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To align with FATF's standards, clause 2 will amend the Casino Control Act to require casino operators to conduct tighter CDD checks on patrons at the point of transaction.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Additionally, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Singapore will be empowered to require casino operators, when conducting CDD checks, to also consider proliferation financing risks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are the risks of financing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, this Bill will enhance the ability of relevant Government agencies to detect and enforce against money laundering through enhanced data sharing, and strengthened prosecutorial levers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Very often, money launderers will conduct and layer their activities across different sectors and use different front entities, so as to avoid detection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When interacting with individual Government agencies, they may leave traces of suspicion, which, on their own, may not raise concerns.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, when triangulated and pieced together with information from other agencies and sources, including Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs), a more revealing picture may emerge.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This can then trigger and support investigations by the relevant law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clauses 18 to 21 introduce amendments to the Income Tax Act, Goods and Services Tax Act, Regulation of Imports and Exports Act, and the Free Trade Zones Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will allow the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office of the Singapore Police Force to augment its analyses of money laundering risks and, in turn, provide richer financial intelligence to law enforcement agencies and AML/CFT regulators for appropriate enforcement action.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The United Kingdom, New Zealand and South Korea have similar tax data sharing arrangements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Likewise, Hong Kong, the United States (US) and Luxembourg have trade data sharing arrangements with their Customs agencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Additionally, clause 10 introduces amendments to the CDSA to allow any AML/CFT regulator, such as the Council for Estate Agencies (CEA) and the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA), to have access to suspicious transactions reports filed by their respective regulated entities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Regulators will then have greater insight into the risks and trends relating to their sectors, and be able to take more effective supervisory and regulatory actions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Guardrails for the data-sharing will be implemented to protect data confidentiality.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Next, we will amend and enhance the levers for prosecution of money laundering cases arising from criminal conduct abroad.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After our investigators painstakingly turn over the stones and uncover the suspects and their activities, the next big challenge is navigating the legal hurdles to successfully prosecute them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To do so, the prosecution needs to show that the monies, allegedly laundered in Singapore, are benefits derived from criminal conduct.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In cases where the criminal conduct is committed outside Singapore, the authorities are currently required to show the complete trail of the monies from the point the crime was committed overseas to the point the monies were deposited with the money launderer in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In many cases, law enforcement agencies face enormous challenges in obtaining the necessary evidence from foreign victims, entities and authorities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is especially so if the criminal proceeds had flowed through many jurisdictions before entering Singapore, which is often the case.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Criminals do this to conceal the origin of their proceeds and exploit such legal requirements to their advantage.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will be sufficient for the prosecution to prove that the money launderer knew or had reasonable grounds to believe that the property he was dealing with were the gains from criminal conduct.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This amendment will significantly alleviate the challenges faced by the prosecution today when dealing with money laundering offences, in cases where the monies laundered had passed through many bank accounts and intermediaries in foreign jurisdictions before entering Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also propose to designate foreign environmental crimes as money laundering predicate offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Currently, law enforcement agencies are only able to investigate money laundering offences arising from the commission of an offence outside Singapore if the foreign offence is also a serious offence under Singapore's laws.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Environmental crimes, such as illegal mining, illegal waste trafficking and illegal logging, are not applicable in our domestic context and, hence, not considered serious offences in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This limits our ability to investigate money laundering associated with such foreign offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, these crimes are one of the largest contributors to transnational organised criminal activities in the East Asia and Pacific region.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is a high propensity for funds arising from such crimes to flow into Singapore, given that we are a well-connected international financial, trading and transit hub.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was highlighted in Singapore's Environmental Crime Money Laundering National Risk Assessment, which we recently published.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amendment will allow the law enforcement agencies to investigate money laundering offences if it is suspected that the monies in Singapore are derived from such serious environmental crimes committed overseas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, this Bill introduces three proposals to improve the processes to deal with seized properties in general, including those linked to money laundering.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Currently, when seized or restrained property is no longer required for investigations or court proceedings, law enforcement agencies must obtain the consent of all parties involved if they want to obtain a court order to sell the property.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is highly impractical because, if there is no consensus amongst the parties, law enforcement agencies will need to continue to manage and maintain the property.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These properties can include vehicles, liquor, luxury watches and livestock.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Not only are they costly to maintain, they also tend to depreciate in value.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The costs of maintenance are borne by the state.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These amendments will allow law enforcement agencies to reduce the cost of property maintenance and preserve the value of seized or restrained properties to facilitate subsequent asset recovery and restitution to the victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also make amendments to deal with properties in cases where the suspect has absconded.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the course of investigations, law enforcement agencies may seize properties linked to persons who are suspected of having committed offences under Singapore's laws but cannot be found despite efforts to reach out to them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In some cases, the persons may have left Singapore and cannot be extradited or refuse to return.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is not uncommon in cross-border financial crimes, such as money laundering and scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Investigations can be wilfully stalled by such absconded persons if they decide to stay out of Singapore in order to avoid being imprisoned for their crimes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But law enforcement agencies need to interview them for the investigations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, the CPC prohibits the Court from releasing a seized property if the property is required for any investigation, inquiry, trial or any proceeding under the law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, if the law enforcement agencies fail to satisfy the Court that any of these grounds for continued seizure of the property applies, the Court may order the property's release or disposal.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the absconded person refuses to return to Singapore, it may become increasingly difficult for the Police, over time, to justify how the continued seizure of the property remains relevant to the investigations, which are not making headway because they cannot interview the person.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This presents an opportunity for absconded persons to frustrate due process.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By staying out of Singapore and, hence, stymying investigations, they have hope that the seized property would eventually be released back to them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Law enforcement agencies can lawfully seize property only where they have reason to suspect that an offence has been committed or the property has some nexus to the offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Further, the Court will also have to determine that the continued seizure will not cause injustice to any person entitled to the possession of the property.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Next, section 372 of the CPC currently provides that if the person entitled to a seized property is unknown or cannot be found, the property will be vested in the Government if no one establishes a claim to it within six months of a public notice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, an absconded person can lay a claim to the property through a legal counsel, while refusing to return to Singapore to cooperate with the investigations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Moreover, absconded persons could try to find creative means to insulate their properties from forfeiture or confiscation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, they could vest the legal title to the properties in other individuals, who may not have committed offences in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These individuals may then present themselves as innocent claimants to the property.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Additionally, clause 16 amends the CPC to provide that the Court may consider whether the property was obtained through legitimate sources, such as income or investments, before the seized property may be released to a third party, even if that third party has not committed any crimes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That party cannot prove his entitlement to the property simply because it was a gift from the absconded person.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To be clear, these amendments continue to be subject to judicial oversight and only affect persons who are suspected to have committed offences in Singapore and have absconded, as well as properties seized in relation to these offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The proposal does not change the existing law or procedures for persons who are not "absconded persons".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Criminals will continue to explore other ways to circumvent even the most stringent of measures, in the fast-changing money laundering landscape.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Singapore will therefore have to continue to be vigilant and we will not hesitate to further tighten our laws against money laundering where necessary, to ensure that our financial and business ecosystem remains reputable and trusted and continues to thrive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As a prominent global financial centre with substantial flows of capital, Singapore faces inherent risks related to money laundering.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is therefore imperative that our anti-money laundering regime remains dynamic and consistently ahead of the evolving tactics of criminals.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These individuals are becoming increasingly sophisticated, employing advanced technology, intricate financial networks and cryptocurrencies to outmaneuver systems of detection and prosecution.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Additionally, amendments will allow STRs filed by entities regulated under CEA and ACRA to be accessed by relevant authorities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Data sharing across Government agencies is a significant step forward.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is the key to seeing the full picture of illicit activities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Like pieces of a puzzle, each agency's data may seem insignificant on its own, but together, they reveal the wider scope of money laundering's operations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The ability to corroborate different sources of data will empower enforcement agencies to identify real threats in the vast number of suspicious transactions filed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Without this collaboration, crucial connections are lost and our understanding of the threat remains fragmented.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, Sir, with the influx of additional data from various agencies, the capability to analyse and make sense of the information must be correspondingly elevated.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will it update its methods, enhance the quality of its intelligence and leverage technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), to help agencies better connect the dots from these diverse sources?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, with improved detection capabilities, how well-resourced are our agencies to respond promptly and effectively to suspected illicit activities?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is crucial that our analytical capabilities and resources keep pace with the increased data flow to ensure we are not overwhelmed with the sheer volume of information, but rather, empowered to act swiftly and decisively.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Second, the Bill expands the toolkit for law enforcement agencies to deal with seized criminal assets.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I support the provision for early sale of seized assets to minimise the cost of property maintenance and preserve the value of these properties.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By streamlining these procedures, law enforcement agencies can act swiftly to order the sale of seized properties, thereby avoiding depreciation or undue costs associated with maintaining these assets.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These provisions are therefore crucial for maintaining the efficiency and effectiveness of our law enforcement agencies and ensuring that justice is both swift and financially responsible.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The unique nature of some seized assets, which can include luxury goods, rare collectibles and high-value personal items, requires specialised knowledge and handling to prevent significant losses during forced sales.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Ensuring that these assets are appropriately appraised and sold through channels that can attract the right buyers at the best possible prices is essential.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This not only maximises the return from these seizures but also reinforces the credibility and efficiency of our asset recovery processes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask whether the current procedures are robust enough to manage these complex and high-value assets effectively.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For instance, how will the authorities market the collectible Bearbrick toy figurines or some 250 luxury handbags and watches to recover the best prices?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Third, I strongly support the provisions in the Bill that allow for the continued seizure of properties in cases where the suspects have absconded and introduce significant barriers to claiming properties linked to these individuals.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Dealing with absconded criminals presents substantial challenges, as jurisdictional issues and international legal complexities often hinder swift justice.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The ability for authorities to seize and maintain control over assets even when the suspect is beyond our reach is therefore crucial.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It disrupts the financial incentives for fleeing, for running away and makes it clear that evading justice will not protect one's ill-gotten gains.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Moreover, by creating legal barriers to claiming properties associated with absconded suspected criminals, we strike at the heart of criminal networks, undermining their financial base and reinforcing the principle that crime does not pay.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These measures are essential for upholding the rule of law and maintaining public confidence in our justice system.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It underscores our commitment to staying ahead of evolving threats by ensuring our legal frameworks remain both robust and adaptive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We address risks head-on as soon as they come to light.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Wealth owners shared that they no longer feel welcomed in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While we are resolute in our commitment in combating money laundering, we must also ensure that our actions reflect the same confidence and clarity that have long defined Singapore as a trusted global financial hub.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By implementing these measures thoughtfully and proportionately, we reinforce that Singapore remains a place where legitimate business thrives and where the integrity of our financial system is safeguarded with both strength and wisdom.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And in doing so, we send a strong message to the world: Singapore is open for business and we welcome those who seek to contribute to our shared prosperity under the rule of law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, if implemented, this Bill is just part of an entire ecosystem that needs to be scrutinised for gaps and vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Member He Ting Ru will speak later about some areas of concern regarding Singapore's ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the 2016 evaluation, Singapore was assessed to have a mostly robust and competent regulatory system when it came to financial institutions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the same could not be said for sectors outside the finance industry, collectively known as designated non-finance businesses and professions (DNFBP).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The DNFBP sectors were noted to lack many of the obligations and supervisions that financial institutions were subject to.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The 2016 evaluation identified that we did not have a strong awareness of illegal fund flows from foreign predicate offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also pointed out that the private sector had weak knowledge of money laundering risks from transnational transactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Fast forward to today, Singapore just published its own Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (ML NRA) report.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This report concurred that there were significant risks in the DNFBP sector which needed to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Last month, this House took a step in the right direction by enhancing the requirements on corporate service providers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Other private sector industries, such as real estate and luxury retail, have rightly been identified as needing to be stepped up too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The money launderers had managed to channel their ill-gotten gains into Singapore with the purpose of washing them through items of tremendously high value.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, just one of the men involved had purchased 10 condominium units at Canninghill Piers worth $85 million, a transaction in which red flags should have been raised.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It has since been reported that some real estate agents were being investigated for giving kickbacks to their clients from the huge commissions earned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is clear then that an effective AML approach needs not just a robust framework.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, Member Dennis Tan will seek clarifications later on the adequacy of AML due diligence measures in the recent cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now move to the Bill before us.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this, I have three queries: (a) on restitution to crime victims; (b) on the change in the law to Jeanette Ang's case; and (c) on STRs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Government's recent paper, National Asset Recovery Strategy 2024, it was stated that the strategy had four operational pillars.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I was pleased to note that under Pillar 3, the strategy aims to "deliver maximum recovery of assets for forfeiture and restitution to victims".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The paper affirmed that Singapore adopted a victim-centric approach towards asset recovery.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I agree that where offenders have profited at the expense of victims, then the assets purchased using such fruits of crime should rightfully be delivered to these victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I, therefore, welcome the provisions, such as clauses 7 and 14 of the Bill, which will help ensure that the value of seized assets is preserved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One challenge regarding delivering restitution to victims is that money laundering is typically transnational in nature.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The victims of crime are often located in other countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the Parliamentary Sitting in July, I had asked whether it would be too late for victims to make claims after a Singapore Court had already forfeited the assets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) had indicated that it would still be open to foreign parties to make requests for MLA even after the Court had made forfeiture orders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For us to assess whether the MLA route is meaningful for victims, could the Ministry confirm how many countries have filed MLA requests with Singapore in the last two years and which three countries have filed the most MLA requests?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to the change in the law arising from Jeanette Ang's case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have a query on the change in clause 11.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 11 will amend the law set out in the 2011 High Court case of Ang Jeanette vs Public Prosecutor to make it easier for the prosecution to prove certain money laundering offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In Jeanette Ang's case, the High Court had ruled that to prove that an accused had committed money laundering, the prosecution needed to show that the monies in the accused's accounts came from criminal conduct.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead, it would simply be sufficient for the prosecution to show that the accused had a guilty frame of mind, that is, that he knew or had reason to believe that the monies came from criminal conduct.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In explaining the rationale for the change, the Ministry pointed to evidentiary difficulties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was said that the proceeds of crime could have been channeled through other bank accounts in other jurisdictions before coming to the accused.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was stated to be difficult to obtain documents from foreign banks to prove the trail of monies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I think earlier, the Minister also touched on this point.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court in that case had stressed the importance of requiring the prosecution to prove the trail of monies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court opined that prosecuting such a mistaken person would not further the purposes of the anti-money laundering conventions and laws.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With the change in clause 11, how will be risk be addressed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: STRs are a key step through which the authorities are alerted to potential money laundering transactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 5 of the Bill will increase the jurisdiction of STRO, that is, the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: STRO will soon be receiving STRs arising from additional legislation, such as the Free Trade Zones Act, Goods and Services Tax Act, Income Tax Act and the Regulation of Imports and Exports Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In order to facilitate the work of STRO, what can we learn from our experience so far about the filing of STRs?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe the numbers are much higher today, a point that Ms Foo Mee Har alluded to earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does that mean that the other 80% were found to be of low quality and not actionable?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, when it came to digital payment tokens (DPTs), a similar trend is being observed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It may also suggest that the STRs are being filed defensively to avoid possible trouble down the road.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Being unclear about the threshold that warrants the filing of an STR harks back to the earlier concerns expressed by FATF about the level of private sector knowledge in Singapore regarding AML risk.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is being done to promote a deeper understanding of what STRs should contain?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to the Ministry's clarifications regarding the three concerns I have raised about restitution to crime victims, the change to the law in the Jeanette Ang case and the quality of STRs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A robust legal framework for AML/CFT is critical in this endeavour.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill consists of proposals across prosecution, foreign environmental crimes, cross-agency data sharing and others.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Taken together with past amendments fronted by MHA, the Ministry of National Development and Ministry of Law (MinLaw), as well as the recently published National Asset Recovery Strategy and updated Money Laundering National Risk Assessment, it underscores an unwavering whole-of-Government emphasis on strengthening our AML/CFT regime amid a dynamic financial crime landscape.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this basis, I support the Bill but would seek some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I will begin with the enhanced levers for prosecution of money laundering cases.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As is, Law Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) are required to show the complete trail of monies from point of crime to deposit in the suspect's account.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A lower bar for prosecution will further deter money mule activities in Singapore while at the same time avail our LEAs with greater capacity to focus on efforts with more systemic outcomes like crippling syndicates with our international partners.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: That said, while the public cheers every successful anti-crime operation by our LEAs, what is foremost on their minds, particularly victims of scams, is how to get their money back.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given that LEAs' efforts on illicit funds tracing would be instrumental in determining their rightful ownership and facilitating their proper seizure for restitution, consistent with one of the four pillars in our National Asset Recovery Strategy, may I seek the Minister's clarification whether the amendment will impact the likelihood of asset recovery for Singaporean victims?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Will these victims have any recourse for cases where investigations reveal an ownership connection but where details of fund flows are unavailable or are no longer required to be pursued for prosecution?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, as it is challenging to obtain information from foreign agencies and entities, international partnerships remain a crucial lever to combat financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will facilitate the greater visibility and timelier confiscation of illicit overseas assets for investigation and restitution to Singapore victims as well as to detain fugitives on the run.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given that Singapore was the FATF president for two years until June 2024, can the Minister also share further plans to boost international cooperation for more robust investigations and asset recovery?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I now turn to clauses 4 and 13 of the Bill, which would empower our LEAs to act upon the criminal proceeds resulting from foreign environmental crimes, which will be listed in the Third Schedule of CDSA.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These proceeds may inevitably flow through Singapore as we are a global financial centre.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to closing the legislative gap highlighted by FATF, this move also signals Singapore's commitment to environmental sustainability on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: First, looking back, can the Minister share the value and number of money laundering cases from environmental crimes that could have been pursued in the past five years had this legislation been in place; and, secondly, clarify if there will, indeed, be retrospective application of this law?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Looking ahead, we may have limited visibility on how these overseas offences evolve.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Other than relying on FATF, can the Minister clarify plans to be more proactive in ensuring the Third Schedule continues to be comprehensive and relevant?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Agencies like CEA and ACRA will also have more access to information.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What is clear from the $3 billion and the other money laundering cases is that, criminals leverage multiple and intertwined points of entry into Singapore's financial ecosystem, be it by asset purchases, shell companies, illegal trade, bank deposits or others.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This risk is expected as with any global financial centre, so the key question is: how can we enhance vigilance across the board, by promoting information sharing, pooling and access to risk insights by both agencies and the private sector.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, in conclusion, Sir, together with the final key amendment on tightening the CDD thresholds for casinos, this Bill will further align our defences against AML/CFT with international best practices and represent progress in safeguarding Singapore's financial integrity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Like my Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) colleague, Ms Sylvia Lim, I support the Bill's objectives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: However, we cannot just react to the immediate circumstances of money laundering cases, but need to more holistically address structural problems at their root to prevent ourselves from being caught out on the back foot.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It would also prevent a situation where our legislation and regulations, which take time, end up having to constantly play catch-up to outlaw new ways in which criminals evolve to launder illicit funds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The challenge of money laundering that we face has several key facets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: First, money laundering can originate from any area within financialised assets, including Single Family Offices (SFOs), cryptocurrencies, fine art and real estate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Second, we would be best served by a comprehensive omnibus AML Bill that consolidates and streamlines the various existing regulations including CFT, CDSA and MAS guidelines.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This unified approach should cover all relevant sectors, including financial institutions to dealers in precious metals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: These laws should also be easily understood by all Singaporeans, not just specialised legal and compliance experts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: An omnibus Bill would present an opportunity to future-proof our legislation by introducing a unifying principle of a duty of financial transparency for our intermediaries, which does not require suspicion of a predicate offence and ensures that Singapore does not become a place that facilitates obfuscation of funds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Third, to effect real change, we must alter the incentive structures to foster a culture of vigilance throughout the financial industry and we should act decisively to establish a whistleblowing fund.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Given the rapid pace of financial innovation and the increasing complexity of corporate structures, we cannot, realistically, stay ahead of all asset classes unless we legislate proactively.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I will focus on three areas not covered by the Bill: SFOs, cryptocurrencies and fine art.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I hope that there can be discussion about the Government's assessment of the risks in these sectors.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It will be insufficient to merely state that these areas are not covered by the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: We must understand how the Government intends to address these areas and ensure that any gaps are effectively closed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Archegos used equity total return swaps to build US$100 billion of portfolio exposure while avoiding disclosure requirements, exposing a significant gap in financial oversight.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: In response, the US is contemplating significant regulatory changes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: These include bringing family offices under the Investment Advisors Act, mandating ownership and business structure disclosures and enhancing trade reporting under the Securities Exchange Act.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Such measures could compel SFOs to provide detailed information about their trades and portfolios.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I strongly advocate for similar advanced disclosure requirements for SFOs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This approach would not only bolster our AML defences, but also curb potential market abuses by SFOs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: We can hit two targets with a single type of policy instrument.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: For SFOs, recent events have demonstrated that SFOs can be a significant conduit for illicit funds entering Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: From 400 in 2020 to about 1,100 by the end of 2022.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This rapid expansion increases the risk of importing financial crimes from jurisdictions with weaker AML controls.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This is a live vulnerability in our AML framework.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The current regulatory landscape presents a glaring gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: SFOs are exempt from MAS legislation or licencing requirements under the SFA, as they do not handle third-party funds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: While this is an MHA Bill, cooperation with MAS is key to addressing the risks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The consultation proposed that all SFOs maintain a relationship with an MAS-regulated financial institution for AML checks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: We have not seen any public updates on actions taken.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: If this public consultation has not been operationalised, then, as stated by the Minister of State Alvin Tan in Parliament on 3 October 2023, only SFOs applying for MAS tax incentives are subject to DDCs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This means, SFOs not seeking tax incentives remain outside our AML framework.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: MAS Managing Director, Mr Chia Der Jiun, stated on 18 July 2024, that Singapore had already issued a set of enhancements for SFOs last year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Can we get more clarity on this statement?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Is this an operationalisation of the July 2023 public consultation?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Currently, SFOs are exempt from many due diligence requirements, allowing their transactions with remittance companies to go largely unscrutinised.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Since 2019, MAS regulations have not required remittance houses to seek prior approval for new customers without face-to-face meetings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Are remittance houses now included in the April 2024 MAS Notice PSN01 (Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Specified Payment Services)?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: If not, what strengthening of remittance house diligence can we expect?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I propose two immediate measures for remittance companies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: First, to introduce cumulative transaction limits for SFOs receiving funds through remittance houses, with an automated system to flag transactions exceeding those limits.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Second, reinstate mandatory face-to-face verification for new customers, especially for high-value or frequent transactions involving SFOs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Cryptocurrencies and other digital assets present unique challenges to our AML efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Crypto is increasingly used to launder proceeds from off-chain crimes, like drug trafficking and fraud, not just crypto-specific crimes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: In 2022 alone, the FBI reported that US victims lost $2.6 billion to pick butchering and other crypto fraud, with the true scale of losses unknown, as victims are often too embarrassed to report crimes to authorities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: While blockchains offer transparency, sophisticated laundering techniques involving multiple transactions and intermediaries pose tracing challenges.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Both centralised exchanges with consolidated wallets and decentralised protocols enable the co-mingling of illicit and legitimate funds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This can take the form of consolidated exchange hot wallets for exchanges, such as Binance; but also decentralise co-minglement protocols through crypto tumblers, such as Tornado Cash; or core protocol features, such as Privacy Coins or Monero's ring signatures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: There is a fundamental tension between crypto's desire for instant, irreversible transactions and the need for financial safeguards.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: While instant transaction finality is desirable in crypto for censorship resistance, it poses risks when it butts up against traditional finance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Our priority must be preserving Singapore's reputation for clean finance over accommodating crypto's preference for irreversibility.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: To address these concerns, we should consider methods like increasing off-ramp fiction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Solutions, could include enhancing scrutiny on crypto-to-fiat conversions, including one-to-three-day escrow periods for large transactions, with the time bought to perform on-chain analysis through providers, like Chainalysis, to check for co-mingled funds or suspicious sources both on centralised exchanges and decentralised protocols.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The art market, with its high value transactions and potential for anonymity, has recently become an attractive avenue for those seeking to launder illicit funds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The 1MDB scandal provides a stark example of how the art market can be exploited.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This includes, Jean-Michel Basquiat's Dust Hits for $48.8 million, along with significant works by Alexander Calder and Mark Rothko.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Low further leveraged these assets, using 17 artworks to collateralise loans worth $107 million from Sotheby's.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Effectively creating additional layers of transactions to obscure the origins of the stolen funds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The scale of this issue is significant and growing with the depth of the market.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: In early 2023, China saw a 14% year-on-year increase in art auction sales to $7.9 billion, with the Old Masters' segment alone rising 15% to $1.1 billion.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The entire global art secured lending space was valued at up to $34 billion in 2023.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This growth in art-related financial services presents new challenges for anti-money laundering efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Collateralised portfolios of art can more easily obscure the origin of funds and complicate scrutiny of wealth sources.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Given these developments, what steps is Singapore taking to address the risks of money laundering through the art market and other alternative assets?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Are we considering implementing AML requirements for auction houses, galleries and art-secured lenders operating in Singapore?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Next, I will move on from individual markets to overarching considerations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This would consolidate the various amendments currently scattered across different acts, including the CFT, CDSA and the numerous MAS guidelines.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Such consolidation would encompass regulations for financial institutions, professionals, trustees and dealers in precious metals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It simplifies compliance for industry professionals and makes our AML laws more accessible to the general public.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Currently, our laws require reporting of suspicious transactions when there are reasonable grounds to suspect criminal activity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Financial institutions and gatekeepers should have an affirmative duty to ensure the transparency of all the transactions they facilitate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This new standard of care would require reasonable efforts to ensure transparency, which is more proactive than our current suspicion-based reporting.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It would involve comprehensive origin and destination checks for funds, verification of the economic rationale for complex transaction structures and enhanced ongoing monitoring for high-risk clients or transactions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The advantage of this approach is that it does not require suspicion of a predicate offence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Instead, it ensures that Singapore does not become a place that facilitates the obfuscation of funds, which some call "Singapore-washing".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: We can protect private wealth without enabling financial opacity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This approach allows us to target the core issue of financial opacity, adapting to new financial instruments and practices as they emerge.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It positions Singapore as a leader in combating global money laundering while maintaining our attractiveness as a financial hub.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Rather than viewing AML measures as mere administrative burdens, we must foster an environment where vigilance is valued and rewarded.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This fund would serve to reward those who come forward with valuable information, with the size of the awards proportional to the value of the assets seized as a result of their disclosures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: In 2023, the US enacted the Anti-Money Laundering Whistleblower Improvement Act as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act 2023.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This legislation, passed unanimously by the Senate, significantly enhances incentives for whistle-blowers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The US experience offers valuable lessons for crafting an effective whistle-blower campaign.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Discretionary awards are rarely paid and have proven ineffective in incentivising whistle-blowers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Confidentiality and anonymity protections allowing whistle-blowers to file complaints anonymously and maintain their anonymity encourage higher participation rates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Compensation for related actions where whistle-blowers are rewarded for enforcement actions by all relevant agencies resulting from their tip promotes comprehensive reporting to all relevant authorities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This cultural issue needs addressing in any regulatory framework.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I believe that a whistle-blower fund, properly implemented, offers us the best shot of changing the game and mindset around suspicious transaction reporting.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: In the fight against money laundering, we will need both carrots and sticks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: While the US already has a strong AML framework, as evidenced by its prosecution of the 1MDB case, it still saw the need to enhance the whistle-blower system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Singapore should follow suit, recognising that motivating individuals to come forward is essential to maintaining a clean and transparent financial system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: By implementing these measures, we can turn the current AML lapses into a catalyst for positive change, fostering a culture of integrity and vigilance within our financial sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The proposed amendments, aimed at enhancing law enforcement capabilities, streamlining asset management and aligning regulatory frameworks with international standards are commendable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I support the Bill's overall objectives, I would like to seek some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, I have some queries with regard to the potential impact on specific groups.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In particular, whilst $4,000 is not an insignificant amount, the much-lowered sum of $4,000 may reduce the attractiveness of the casinos to tourists.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may be put off by the additional due diligence process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister provide data or studies that justify this reduction and its projected impact on these stakeholders?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should find a balance between allowing the genuine punters who are here to enjoy the thrill of gambling versus those who are here to game the system and wash their ill-gotten gains in criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, we will be suffocating the very clients who are essential to the casinos to keep afloat and contribute to the tourism traffic in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, the money launderers from the recent high-profile cases or convictions know that they will keep a wide berth from using Singapore as their playground.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is no lack of alternatives in the region for them to move around.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, while I understand the necessity of robust customer due diligence measures, I am also mindful of the potential operational challenges and financial burden these measures may impose, particularly on smaller enterprises.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments proposed rigorous customer due diligence measures for casinos and other entities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Understanding the rationale and considerations behind implementing such stringent measures across diverse business sizes is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, the success of this Bill hinges not only on the strength of its provisions, but also on the effectiveness of its implementation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill emphasises coordination amongst various Ministries and agencies, such as the Gambling Regulatory Authority which oversees the Casino Control Act, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the framework designed to facilitate this interagency collaboration?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, while I recognise the necessity of information sharing to combat financial crime, it is critical to ensure that individual privacy is protected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill also addresses the sharing of information among Suspicious Transaction Reporting Officers and regulatory bodies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What safeguards are in place to protect individuals' privacy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure that the information shared is used solely for its intended purpose?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is there a timeline when information shared needs to be destroyed after its intended use?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given the sensitive nature of financial data, I believe it is paramount to address any potential privacy concerns comprehensively.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mr Speaker, Sir, it is important to understand how we measure up to international standards and best practices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill aims to align with recommendations from FATF.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, it would be valuable to understand how Singapore's approach compares with international best practices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sixth, Mr Speaker, Sir, it is essential to ensure that the measures introduced in this Bill remain effective in the face of constantly evolving financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What mechanisms are in place to review the effectiveness of the new measures and make necessary adjustments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Regular evaluation will ensure that the legislation remains relevant and effective in combating evolving financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This year alone, we have seen a slew of Bills introduced to tackle various aspects of financial crime, demonstrating our unwavering dedication to this critical issue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Despite these Bills, we have also seen a rise in the number of people wanted for money laundering and financial fraud in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I commend the Government for its efforts in introducing this Bill, I believe that it is essential to carefully consider the potential impact on specific groups, ensure operational feasibility and cost-effectiveness and establish robust safeguards for privacy and data protection.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A thorough understanding of the comparative analysis with international best practices and the implementation of robust evaluation and review mechanisms will further strengthen this Bill and ensure its long-term effectiveness in safeguarding Singapore's financial integrity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is, therefore, important that the right lessons are learnt and applied, and laws and procedures are enhanced to prevent or minimise similar cases in future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We read that, and I quote, "millions of dollars earned over the years from an illicit gambling ring were turned into luxury cars, extravagant watches, properties in Singapore's most lavish neighbourhoods, jewellery, designer goods, cryptocurrency and cold hard cash".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So far, we read of media reports of kickbacks received by property agents or bankers taking cuts for property purchases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But the purchase of these properties required various parties or professionals who should be obligated to do AML due diligence checks required by the authorities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The money launderers could have brought monies into Singapore either by cash or by remitting monies to Singapore via their existing bank accounts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Where money was remitted to bank accounts in Singapore, the banks located in Singapore would have had the chance to do their AML due diligence searches.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For those who bought real estate here, besides the banks, the real estate agents as well as the conveyancing lawyers would have been required to do AML due diligence checks, including especially on the source of funds they put up for payment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And if so, what were the authorities' responses to such reports?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The programme aims to ensure that RFAs are well equipped to comply with AML/CFT regulations through continuous education.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: RFAs have to fulfil the new requirements once every two years as a precondition for their renewal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I passed the test but, subsequently, I did not remain an RFA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, the course and the test left me with deep impressions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, while strict adherence can be onerous, if all professionals and service providers were to take the AML due diligence checks seriously and conscientiously, one would have thought that they would greatly help to prevent, or at least to minimise, the bringing in or the utilisation of funds which are subject to prohibitions under the AML regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So far, not much is directly disclosed about AML due diligence efforts of the bankers, property agents, lawyers or other service providers or sales agents who serve or assisted the convicted members of the $3 billion money laundering case.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.31 pm until 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With my past experience as the head of a leading local stockbroking company, I am aware of the challenges and temptations faced by financial institutions with regard to money laundering.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) welcomes the move by the Government to enhance the legal framework for preventing, investigating and prosecuting money laundering offences through this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our nation's reputation as a rule-based financial centre has taken a great hit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As one of the premier financial hubs in Asia, we are structurally exposed to money laundering.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: People from all over the world want to park their money here because they know that their money will be safe.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has created huge economic benefits for our financial industry and PSP recognises this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we want the money to be legitimate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Integrity is the most enduring competitive advantage for a global financial centre.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that even if the trade-off for taking a tougher stance against money laundering is slower growth of our financial services industry in the short term, it is a worthy trade-off in the long term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be sufficient for the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the money launderer knew, or had reasonable grounds to believe, that he was dealing with criminal proceeds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a step in the right direction, which will enhance the prosecution's ability to pursue and prosecute money launderers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I am also concerned whether this will also lead to banks adopting an overly cautious approach towards restricting or closing bank accounts out of concern for potential legal consequences, thus hindering legitimate transactions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Ministry envision any safeguards to protect legitimate customers who may be inevitably caught in such a scenario?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also support the move to reduce the threshold for casino operators to perform customer due diligence when they enter into cash transactions with patrons or receive deposits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, at the same time, I would like to know whether there is a maximum cap on the amount of cash that a casino can accept in one transaction.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, are our casinos allowed to take in cash exceeding $1 million in one go?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We maintain the mandatory death penalty for serious drug trafficking offences because of the immense harm caused to drug abusers, their families and the community.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But are we doing enough to punish money launderers who may be trying to conceal money which originated from drug trafficking or other serious illegal activities?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, there have been an increasing number of Singaporeans being caught for being money mules.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In many cases, they handed over their bank accounts and private information in exchange for small amounts of money, usually in the range of hundreds of dollars each time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of these offenders have been sentenced to imprisonment for periods of two to three months for their offences.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In comparison, the offenders of the $3 billion money laundering case got to enjoy a luxurious lifestyle worth millions of dollars in Singapore for several years before they were caught.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the jail terms of 13 to 17 months proportional to the crimes they have committed, when compared to those of the money mules?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be appropriate for me to ask at this juncture this question.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With money laundering in the billion-dollar scale only attracting up to 17 months of imprisonment, what sort of money laundering crimes did the Government envision would potentially attract the maximum imprisonment sentences under Part VI of the CDSA?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Inter-Ministerial Committee Reviewing Singapore's Anti-Money Laundering Regime will publish its full findings and recommendations in the fourth quarter.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP hopes that one of its recommendations will be to strengthen the sentencing regime and increase the deterrent effect against money laundering by way of imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We understand that MHA most recently reviewed the adequacy of the prescribed penalties against money laundering only in 2023.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we believe that the sentencing regime should be reconsidered, given the relatively short jail terms that were handed down to those who had been caught in one of the largest anti-money laundering operations worldwide.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I also ask the Minister if the Sentencing Advisory Panel will consider issuing an advisory on the sentencing framework for offences under the CDSA based on the lessons learnt from the $3 billion money laundering case?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Following the review of the Inter-Ministerial Committee, we hope we will further strengthen the penalties against banks, other financial institutions and their senior management who contravened anti-money laundering rules.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Fellow Singaporeans, the $3 billion money laundering case has severely damaged our country's reputation as an international financial center and has had adverse effects on our society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP supports the Government in amending several related laws following the money laundering case, including the CDSA Bill being discussed today, to strengthen our enforcement efforts against money laundering.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that the most important aspect of the anti-money laundering regime is proper sentencing.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I also believe the importance of this Bill in strengthening anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing measures can improve trade relations with other countries, as partners will have greater trust in Singapore's regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s compliance with the recommendations made by the Financial Action Task Force will increase confidence among international investors and financial institutions and help attract more foreign capital.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This is quite evident from the healthy inflow of investments we continue to see, as reported in in the recent announcements by the Economic Development Board (EDB) and by the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI).

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: By cracking down on illicit activities, the Bill helps protect legitimate businesses from being undermined by unfair competition from entities engaged in money laundering or financing terrorism.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the Bill may also lead to development of new services and products in the financial sector such as advanced compliance software, consulting services, and anti-money laundering and counter terrorism financing training programmes.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Compliance costs may also increase substantially leading to closure of some SME businesses.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While some consolidation in this sector may be necessary there is also a risk that overly stringent regulations might stifle innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses might be hesitant to engage in new ventures or adopt innovative practices due to the fear of non-compliance or excessive regulatory scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Are there any exemptions for small businesses or any specific sub-sectors?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, are there any transitional provisions provided to help businesses adjust to these new requirements?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, how do our regulations align with international AML/CTF standards and the recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Are there any specific international guidelines that businesses should be aware of?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, could you please also clarify the procedures and measures for ensuring privacy and security of collected customer data?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has a comprehensive Anti-Money Laundering Regime centered around the three pillars of prevention, detection and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill helps us to continue to be responsive to new threats in the future that threatens the status and confidence in Singapore as an international financial hub.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the first amendment, the law as it currently stands requires the Prosecution to prove that property or assets are benefits of criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is quite difficult to do especially in sophisticated financial transactions, with layers after layers of sophisticated transactions, across various jurisdictions and split over different amounts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some are even converted into other types of assets to further mask the transactions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will be tough to conduct the tracing exercise to the predicate offence which usually occurs overseas.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, even if the account or asset holder admits that he or she has acted as a money mule or has given up control of the account to receive and transfer such illicit funds, that alone may not be enough to prosecute.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Jurisdictions like Hong Kong, Canada and Australia have already done away with such requirement to prove that the property or asset in question came from or are benefits of the criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And that it is not presumed that the accused is in receipt of illicit funds just because the last transfer of monies went into his or her account.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is this to be referenced similarly to an objective test as to whether or not he or she ought to have known that such monies were criminal proceeds?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially important for seized assets like vessels or specialised items.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my previous experience as a maritime lawyer, I arrest vessels to secure maritime lien and admiralty claims on behalf of clients and if no release has been made, then through the Sheriff, the arrested vessels will be put up for sale.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the process will be long and expensive.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While the vessel is still under arrest and if the owner has abandoned the vessel, the arresting party has to foot the bills for the wages and sustenance of the crew, security guards, repairs and maintenance, bunkering costs, insurance coverage, port dues, and many other expenses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And the longer the vessel sits under the arrest, the higher the exposure of liability on the arresting party.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, in one case that I had, the Master or the captain of the vessel, fell and suffered a chipped tooth and needed medical attention.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In another case, a homesick crew with special extenuating circumstances had to be repatriated and change of crew had to be made.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All of these means more costs and risks will be saddled on the arresting party.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We cannot have the same situation saddled on our law enforcement agencies as this will be a burden on taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For specialised items that are being seized, they also may require special storage with the right temperature and humidity conditions to ensure that the value and veracity of the items are preserved.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Handbags, watches and other high luxury items fall into such category.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is this in terms of percentage of the value of the seized assets?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will MHA look at setting a standard threshold set for the costs of maintenance in terms of percentage of the value of the seized assets, beyond which it will be unfeasible to continue to retain those assets under seizure because this then will provide clear guidance?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, what are the safeguards to balance the rights on interested parties in the assets?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, will ample notice be given by way of advertisement to ensure that any interested parties can attend the Court hearing to be heard before the sale of the assets?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, before determining that such assets can be sold, what are the steps that can be taken to ensure that any evidential value from the property or asset has been extricated and preserved?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, through the cloning of any metadata, photographs and videos of the assets, anything and everything that may have evidentiary value to the investigations must already been taken, before such assets can be sold.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, will the relevant law enforcement agencies consult industry valuation experts who are familiar with such properties or assets to determine the risk of depreciation?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fifthly, what are the safeguards to ensure that the sale of the seized assets is for the right value and made to genuine purchasing parties.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, in the standard Sheriff’s Condition for Sale of vessels, the Court's approval will be required to sanction any accepted bids below the appraised value.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, what are the safeguards to ensure that the value of the seized assets continue to be protected even after the sale order has been made?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, it will be better to approach a calibrated sale rather than flooding the market with many items, all being put up to auction all at once.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Alternatively, married deals through specialised auction houses for a specific group of accredited bidders, can be made to ensure the exclusivity of the offer and higher bid returns.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, on third parties' claims to properties linked to absconded persons.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: No longer can such parties hide behind the excuse that these ill-gotten gains are gifts made to them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In any case, the common law principles of presumption of advancement or gift still apply to family members like spouses or children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, it is incumbent upon this group of third parties to prove that if the assets are not gifts, how are they able to afford the assets with regard to their own income, revenue or savings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do have a small clarification in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In law, there is the concept of "equity's darling" – a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, family members or friends who are truly not proxies need not fear this amendment if they can show how they gave value to the acquisition and how they came into ownership of such asset.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, what about gifts or donations made or pledged to charities or foundations with a social cause?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will such assets be clawed back, given that they are linked to the absconded persons?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a previous response to the Parliament, MHA has explained that the forfeited assets and cash will go to the Consolidated Funds.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, in Australia, the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 establishes a scheme to confiscate proceeds of crime and allows for such confiscated funds to be used to benefit the community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is also a call for a grant to be provided for deserving programmes under such a scheme.
