speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If Singapore has a similar lever, then such assets that have been pledged or donated to charities that are recognised and accredited in Singapore can also stand to benefit those charities, assuming that the charities played no part in the commission of the offence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would not dwell into the specifics of the particular case, but suffice to say, with billions of dollars involved, many are questioning how this could happen in Singapore, what measures can be taken to prevent a recurrence and whether our current safeguards are adequate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am glad that this Bill, amongst many others, would strengthen our stance on anti money laundering.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the one hand, the arrest of the individuals involved in these money laundering activities, despite their complex cross-border operations, instils confidence in the capabilities of our Police Force to handle such intricate cases.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the other hand, it underscores the need for more robust measures to prevent money laundering crimes and to empower our law enforcement agencies to seek justice more effectively when a crime has been committed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, the proposed amendments to the Bill are crucial.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They aim to enhance the ability of our law enforcement agencies to pursue and prosecute money laundering offences and to clarify and improve our processes for dealing with seized or restrained properties linked to suspected criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These steps are vital for strengthening our anti money laundering efforts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a welcomed change as it enables the prosecution of money mules in cases where money is laundered through bank accounts and intermediaries in foreign jurisdictions before entering Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will we address situations where money launderers use innocent, unaware victims within Singapore to deceive and mislead investigators?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we ensure adequate protection for these innocent victims?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have encountered cases where the bank accounts of suspected mules were frozen for months, only to be cleared of any wrongdoings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In some instances, their accounts remain frozen for over three months, leaving them without access to their funds.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we better protect innocent victims in such scenarios?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is the threshold for the depreciation in value of the properties for the Court to order their sale?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In cases where the seized properties are vehicles, does this then imply that the vehicles should be sold off as soon as possible to recover the maximum value?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They aim to enhance the ability of our law enforcement agencies to pursue and prosecute money laundering offences.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we must also ensure that the amendments to the Bill are implemented effectively and justly, safeguarding the interests of innocent parties while enhancing our anti money laundering efforts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Does the revised law allow banks to hold assets for a certain number of days after a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) is filed, so that the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office (STRO) can decide whether to issue a seizure order?When a customer instructs a bank to make a payment and the bank holds the transaction pending STRO approval, how does the law prevent tipping off the customer that an STR has been filed, which could prejudice ongoing investigations?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Regarding the proposal to allow Government agencies to share information and data with one another, it must be done, in order to facilitate and expedite investigations and prosecution.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I have some concerns about this arrangement too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government ensure data privacy and security with the increased sharing of sensitive tax and trade data information?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will there be a heightened risk of shared data misuse and, if so, what preventive measures will be in place to mitigate this risk?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister share which specific challenges are anticipated in the process to prove that the individuals knew they were dealing with criminal proceeds and how will these be addressed?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We also need to provide training and resources to law enforcement agencies to handle the complexities of international money laundering cases.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I strongly support the proposal to allow the Court to order the sale of seized or restrained properties linked to suspected criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What procedures will be put in place to ensure fair and transparent sale of the seized assets?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry ensure a transparent process for the valuation and sale of seized assets?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will public auctions or third-party assessments be conducted?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the proceeds from the sale of seized properties can be used to support victims and further crime prevention efforts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What support will be provided to casino operators to comply with the new regulations?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry also consider a phased approach to give casinos time to adjust their processes and systems?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore plays a pivotal role as a global financial hub.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, our financial regulations should align with international standards to preserve our reputation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a critical aspect of our commitment to global financial integrity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also recognise that these amendments' roles in fortifying our defences against illicit activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These enhancements, along with previous amendments, bolster our enforcement capabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They also provide us with the tools needed to effectively combat bad actors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, the successes of these measures depends on their implementation and the perceptions of those responsible for their enforcement, especially our compliance officers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to ensure these regulations are communicated.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Compliance officers must have an accurate understanding of the intents and specifications of the various AML amendments and avoid taking an overly-conservative approach that places excessive compliance burdens.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Striking a balance is essential, as being too strict or too lenient can be detrimental.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Excessive conservatism can stifle legitimate financial activities, deter investment inflows and negatively impact job creation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, compliance officers must find a middle ground that ensures regulatory compliance without imposing unnecessary constraints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This introduces friction for individuals trying to establish entitlement to properties linked to absconded persons.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are concerns that these new laws might deter legitimate investments and businesses, particularly, by increasing the risk of property seizure, impacting investments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While we understand the necessity of these amendments, there is a perception that they may confer excessive power on the Police to seize properties without due Court process.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This raises questions about the impact on the perception on foreign investors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important to consider the psychological aspect.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Singapore, we enjoy a high trust in our society and law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This may make these measures seem fair to our citizens.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, foreign investors may come from societies with lower trust in similar institutions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, how can we assuage concerns from our international investors regarding these powers?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Next, I would like to address a significant issue related to compliance, particularly within the financial and real estate sectors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is feedback from the ground, including private bankers, that compliance officers are interpreting regulations with an overly-conservative approach.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, a client who has purchased a property and received the Temporary Occupation Permit is now being retroactively asked to prove the source of funds.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, investors are questioning whether real estate developers can depend on the Know Your Client (KYC) and due diligence conducted by banks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This cautious approach can sometimes seem excessive and it has led to perception that Singapore is becoming an onerous place for investment and that Singapore is no longer open for business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the measures in this Bill and the four AML-related amendments enacted since May 2023, there is a concern that this could unduly increase the compliance burden on our industries, particularly in finance and real estate.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important to note that compliance officers in different industries have varied timelines to adjust to new regulations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the finance industry has had a longer period to develop KYC policies, compared to the real estate industry.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is also a concern about uneven standards of personal data protection.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, we need to support these industries in levelling up their compliance practices for consistent application.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, could we provide clear guidance to compliance officers to ensure they do not adopt overly conservative approaches that could deter investment and hinder our economic growth?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, they must not, inadvertently, create a heavier compliance load or foster negative perceptions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While we aim to strengthen our defences against illicit activities, our approach should also foster a dynamic economic environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since then, the last of the 10 offenders have been convicted and deported from Singapore just last week.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I am sure most of my Parliamentary colleagues would agree with the principle behind this Bill – to enhance and clarify our powers to combat attempts to use Singapore's trusted reputation for illegal activities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I would like to take the opportunity to seek the Minister's clarifications on the implementation of a tighter AML, terrorism financing (TF) and proliferation financing (PF) regime.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the Ministerial Statements regarding the billion-dollar money laundering case last year, it was announced that an Inter-Ministerial Committee, comprising officeholders across MAS and various Ministries, would look into keeping our AML regime up-to-date.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The latest announcement was that the Inter-Ministerial Committee is due to share its full findings and recommendations in the fourth quarter of 2024.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there a special urgency for the measures that are proposed in this Bill?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As was pointed out in the Ministerial Statements of October 2023, we must avoid a "knee-jerk" reaction to the billion-dollar case.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must balance any responsive measures with the consideration that there are still legitimate business and fund flows, which we do not want to unduly impede.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With that consensus, would it be more expedient to consider our AML strategy in the round after the Inter-Ministerial Committee's findings and recommendations are known?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That way, we can fashion a more holistic update of our regime, as compared to making piecemeal tweaks at various times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That would also allow businesses and investors to undertake a single review of their operations and compliance policies and keep compliance costs competitive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should ensure that they do not come across as arbitrary.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How much more have been spent to store, maintain and safeguard properties, vehicles and luxury goods to date?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the amount of depreciation suffered from the time that the various assets were seized?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How much of the seized assets have yet to be appropriated to the consolidated fund for Government use?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister please clarify, what circumstances would fall under the "interests of justice" limb?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If these proposed powers were available in 2023, for example, what are the types of assets which would have been sold after they were seized in the billion-dollar case?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that the Bill also contains new provisions to prevent absconded persons from making successful claims to seized properties.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the value of seized properties that absconded individuals have been able to make away with and how have they managed to obtain delivery of such properties from the authorities despite being absent from jurisdiction?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Clause 11 of the Bill also seeks to make it easier for the Prosecution to prove a money laundering offence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Prosecution will no longer need to provide the full chain of how the monies laundered in Singapore are traced to the benefits or gains from criminal conduct, as long as they can show that the money launderer knew or had reasonable grounds to believe that the person was dealing with the benefits from criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does this mean that someone can be criminally liable as a money launderer if he mistakenly believes that he is dealing with ill-gotten gains, or must the monies dealt with still need to be attributable to criminal conduct?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If it is the latter, what would be the standard of proof required?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This change comes slightly a year after we had tightened our laws to act against money mules, who sell or use their payment and Singpass accounts for criminals to receive or transfer money.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill also introduces amendments to allow Government agencies to share tax data and trade data with Singapore's Financial Intelligence Unit, the STRO of CAD.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sectoral regulators, such as the CEA and ACRA, will also be given access to STRs filed by their respective regulated entities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As explored in the clarifications to the Ministerial Statements last year, the key is not in an indiscriminate blasting of the confidential STRs to anyone who wants them, but to be clear about who is the central node who is making sense of all the STRs and the data that is being reported and fed to.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Who will play the role of this central node or do we envisage a semi-decentralised system where different regulators keep an eye on different scopes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there merit in setting up a central coordination point like the Anti-Scam Centre does for our scam-fighting efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An effective solution must harness an ability to access information across different spheres.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would include the developed system of STRs that are now regularly filed by our financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The concern is that it may lead to higher risks of seizures and impact wealth flows.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I look forward, Mr Speaker, to seeing the Inter-Ministerial Committee's findings and recommendations later this year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among other things, I think it is key to our AML objectives to focus on parts of the ecosystem that have not been regulated or as closely regulated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, high-value assets, such as luxury cars, bags and liquor, do not have the same structural regulation as financial instruments and real estate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But these are beyond the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a positive move that will strengthen both our ability to address the transnational nature of money laundering operations and tighten our internal anti-money laundering processes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point, is on the lower threshold for the prosecution of money laundering cases arising from criminal conduct abroad.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rationale provided by the Ministry for removing the physical element is to remove the impediment that law enforcement agencies currently face in obtaining evidence from victims, entities and authorities outside jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To address evidential difficulties, there are other legal mechanisms, such as rebuttable legal presumptions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share why the Ministry considered legal presumptions to be insufficient for addressing the evidential difficulties, such that it had to resort to removing the physical element altogether?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, it is a defence if a defendant can raise a reasonable doubt as to whether the money laundered in Singapore were, in fact, benefits from criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the defendants in such cases may be money mules, who may have limited resources and access to financial institutions, can the Minister share examples of how practically a defendant might be able to show reasonable doubt?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I previously filed PQs on classifying wildlife crimes as serious offences in the Organised Crime Act 2015.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On 5 October 2020, the Ministry said that no links with corruption, money laundering or fraud were established for cases of illegal wildlife trade in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On 2 November 2021 and 7 November 2022, the Ministry said that, where illegal wildlife trade seizures involve entities outside of Singapore, our enforcement agencies work closely with the source and destination countries and share information with international organisations, such as the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora and INTERPOL.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In removing the physical element for prosecuting money laundering cases, the Ministry explained that documents from financial institutions of foreign countries to prove the trail of monies are dependent on the cooperation of foreign entities, which is often difficult to secure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is it the case, then, when no links were found between illegal wildlife trade and money laundering when cooperating with entities outside of Singapore, we were working on the basis of inadequate evidence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the amendments, then, allow us to more proactively tackle environmental crimes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond prosecuting money mules, can the Minister confirm that tracing the financial trails to prosecute the masterminds and kingpins behind these operations will remain a priority?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If documents from financial institutions are difficult to secure, what other steps are being taken to improve the flow of information between countries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point, is on the proposed sharing of data between Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The data that is obtained by STRO may be passed on to the AGC or other prosecuting agencies for use in prosecutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The information may, then, emerge in open court trials.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what safeguards are in place when data is passed from one agency to another?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If a prosecution is brought based on evidence obtained by STRO from other agencies, would the data still be treated as confidential?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Prosecution apply to Court to redact or seal the documents?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or would the public interest in an open hearing mean that the information will no longer be treated as confidential?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what factors STRO will consider in deciding what data to share with regulators?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the purposes and limits on STRO's power to share data with regulators?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what happens to the data after there is no longer a need for STRO or regulators to possess the data?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, if it is determined, after investigations, that no wrongdoing has been committed, will STRO and regulators permanently delete the data obtained?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If data is retained, what is the retention period for this data and where will the data be stored?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on the sale of seized or restrained properties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One scenario where the court can do so is if the property is likely to be subject to depreciation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the law enforcement agencies will determine if the value of the property is likely to depreciate?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What factors or framework will be used by said agencies to determine the expected value of the property?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be a specific timeframe set by the agencies to determine the expected valuation of property within that timeframe?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the agencies seek the assistance or expertise of professionals in determining the valuation of more niche assets?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One example of a highly volatile asset in today's landscape is cryptocurrency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will law enforcement agencies determine the valuation of a defendant's cryptocurrency wallet, which is highly volatile?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has stated that the powers relating to the sale of properties is to enhance restitution to victims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister consider detailing how the proceeds of sales will be used for victim restitution?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What factors will determine whether an individual qualifies to receive restitution?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, what is the process for an individual to receive said restitution?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fourth and final point, is on the designation of foreign environmental crimes as money laundering predicate offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Defining and addressing wildlife crimes as transnational crimes is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have previously spoken up about this suggestion, as the close links between wildlife crime and other organised crimes, such as drug trafficking and money laundering, constitutes a serious threat to public safety in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This measure would empower our local enforcement agencies to effectively tackle wildlife crime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, it would have a strong signalling and deterrence effect against wildlife crime, both in Singapore and globally.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This legislation aims to fortify our financial system against the threats of money laundering, terrorism financing and the financing of weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore, known for its clean and transparent financial hub, remains a target for malicious actors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill proposes crucial amendments to the CDSA to simplify the prosecution of money laundering cases, particularly those with international ties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, prosecutors must establish a direct link between criminal conduct and laundered money in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is extremely challenging when funds move across multiple jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Prosecutors must, of course, still demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt, that the accused knew or had reason to believe that they were handling criminal proceeds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This amendment strikes a necessary balance between facilitating prosecution and protecting individual rights.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, the subjective nature of the "reasonableness" standard requires careful monitoring.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would the Ministry be guided in determining what constitutes "reasonableness"?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the precedent cases and judgments that would guide the Ministry?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This move is timely, reflecting the global urgency to combat environmental degradation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Offenses, like illegal mining, logging and waste trafficking, will now be recognised as serious offenses under our laws, aligning Singapore with international efforts to protect the environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To ensure effective enforcement, I ask the Ministry to clarify the measures it will implement to foster international cooperation in investigating these offenses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Establishing partnerships with global environmental agencies and enhancing information-sharing protocols will be essential.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill also emphasises the importance of enhanced cross-agency data sharing to improve the detection of money laundering activities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Amendments to various Acts will enable agencies, such as IRAS and Customs to share data with STRO.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Given the increasing complexity of financial crimes, real-time data sharing is vital for timely intervention and regulatory action.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Considering the recent data breaches, the Ministry must ensure that robust data privacy and security measures are in place within this framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Strengthening data security protocols and conducting regular audits will be crucial to protecting sensitive information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A key aspect of the Bill is the focus on leveraging technology to combat money laundering and other financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technologies, like artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain and advanced data analytics, offer significant potential to enhance transaction monitoring and regulatory oversight.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister also share, how does the Ministry intend to use these technologies and to outline plans for further integration?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill also amends the Casino Control Act to tighten requirements for casino operators regarding CDD checks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These changes align our regulations with international standards, ensuring that our casino sector remains resilient against money laundering and terrorism financing threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it is also important to balance these new requirements with operational feasibility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I suggest that the Ministry also consider a phased approach to introducing these requirements, accompanied by industry feedback sessions and consultations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement is ready to assist with any education or awareness sessions required.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This phased implementation will help a smooth transition while upholding robust AML/CFT standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will respond to their speeches in two parts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first part will be on the broad themes that they raised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second part will be on specific questions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One broad theme concerns the robustness of Singapore's anti-money laundering, or AML, regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members acknowledge that the Bill would further strengthen our regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some, like Ms He Ting Ru, advocate for more proactive legislation, although it is not clear, how much in advance, proactive means.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, Members, like Mr Edward Chia, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and even Mr Leong Mun Wai, worry about the signal to legitimate investors and businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In astronomy, there is a sweet spot known as the "Goldilocks Zone" where planets are orbiting at a distance from a star that is "just right".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Any closer to the star and water on that planet turns into steam.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Neither scenario will support life as we know it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Though just a character in a children's story, Goldilocks' famous approval of things that are "just right" has been applied many times over, including in regulations, to describe the desire to strike a right balance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Is our AML regime within the "Goldilocks Zone", enough to deter criminals but not so much as to drive away legitimate investors?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Here are some facts that strongly suggest that we are "in the zone".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A broad range of factors was considered, including "Political Stability and Rule of Law" and "Institutional and Regulatory Environment".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The financial sector contributes to about 13% of our GDP and employs about 200,000 of our people in good paying jobs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is also important for sustaining Singapore's vibrant business environment and growth in other sectors, such as legal and professional services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the last Mutual Evaluation of Singapore in 2016, FATF assessed Singapore to have a strong legal and institutional framework to fight money laundering, with highly sophisticated coordination involving all relevant authorities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While Singapore had achieved strong outcomes in some areas, FATF recommended improvements in others, such as DNFBPs, for example.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Notwithstanding its recommendation, FATF's overall assessment of Singapore puts us in good company.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The handout I had circulated earlier contains some further details that show this clearly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Neil Parekh and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how our AML regime compares internationally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We share Mr Yip's view that interagency coordination is critical for the successful implementation of our AML measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To achieve this, we have established interagency mechanisms, such as the AML/CFT Steering Committee, co-chaired by the relevant Permanent Secretaries of MHA, the Ministry of Finance and MAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The fight against money laundering is a journey without end and our measures cannot come as one burst of fire with no further heat applied to the problem areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is, in fact, how we have worked in the past and how we will need to work in the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Mr Saktiandi's question, we did not time this Bill to respond to any specific case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We continually review and tighten our regime in response to new threats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Mr Dennis Tan's question on what lessons have been learnt from the recent money laundering case, I have dealt with this comprehensively in my Ministerial Statement last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members will also recall that in April, we launched COSMIC, a digital platform which MAS co-developed with the major banks to allow financial institutions to share information with one another on customers whose behaviours are indicative of financial crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In June, we updated our Money Laundering National Risk Assessment as part of our ongoing efforts to raise awareness and guide all stakeholders to better detect key money laundering risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are pushing ahead with this Bill because it has been in the making for about two years and there is no value to hold it back once the work is done.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Should the IMC recommend further measures that require legislative updates, we will plan for them to be enacted as soon as practicable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, it is critical to our success as an international financial centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We cannot be competitive if financial services are poorly regulated or if financial institutions and other gatekeepers here are inadequately supervised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Legitimate investors and asset managers will not feel sufficiently protected to flow their capital through Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the other hand, poorly designed regulations will not keep out illicit money flows and may instead turn away legitimate businesses, to our detriment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More regulation and, sometimes, proactive legislation, do not always equal effective protection – we must be clear about that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In short, we have zero tolerance towards criminals who exploit our financial system and have sought to get our AML regime "just right" by taking a risk-based approach in line with the FATF standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means that we must have a good understanding of the risks we face, including emerging trends and developments that are being exploited by criminals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To prevent, detect and enforce against their illicit activities, we developed tools and frameworks which are fit-for-purpose, proportionate to the risks and effective.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Guided by the principle of responding appropriately to risk, we have established a strong track record of providing a stable and predictable environment for businesses to thrive and investors to manage their wealth here.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will not change with the passage of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chia, Ms Foo, Mr Parekh and Mr Saktiandi raised concerns about potential increases in compliance costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They seek to improve our law enforcement agencies' abilities to detect and enforce against illicit activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The amendments will also not impose undue friction nor burden for legitimate businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, we made it a priority to ensure that they are reasonable and practicable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nonetheless, I thank Members for raising concerns about knee-jerk reactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is not surprising to see financial intermediaries heighten compliance checks after major cases, especially in the sectors which the money launderers exploited.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such vigilance is not a bad thing in and of itself.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Gatekeepers do have an outsized role in our collective defence against money laundering.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, aligned with our overall approach towards money laundering, these checks need to be sensible and calibrated and not unduly impede legitimate businesses and investors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Sectoral regulators will continue to engage and work with the gatekeepers in the respective industries to level up compliance capabilities and to strike the right balance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This approach also applies to the sectors which Ms He Ting Ru raised in her speech, namely, single family offices, cryptocurrency and fine art.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While we do not disagree with the need to be vigilant, ultimately, what serves us best is a risk-based approach, which we have taken.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means not viewing all transactions with suspicion but looking into instances of concern.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Don Wee, Mr Saktiandi and Mr Yip asked about the lowered threshold for customer due diligence checks, or CDD checks, and its impact on casino operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Other FATF jurisdictions are similarly expected to impose the same CDD threshold on their casino operators.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While this would increase the number of CDD checks on patrons, it is unlikely to deter bona fide patrons from visiting the two casinos or affect their competitiveness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Mr Leong's question, while there are no limits to the amount that casinos can accept, casino operators will be required to conduct the necessary CDD checks, and be satisfied that the funds are from legitimate sources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum also asked about educating and supporting the casinos in tackling proliferation financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The casino operators have already put in place processes to prevent and detect proliferation financing in line with FATF standards, such as monitoring of patrons for proliferation financing risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Gambling Regulatory Authority had consulted the casino operators on the revised CDD threshold and upcoming requirements to mitigate proliferation financing and they did not raise any concerns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Choo, Mr Derrick Goh, Ms Foo, Mr Louis Ng, Assoc Prof Razwana, Mr Saktiandi, Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Wee and Mr Dennis Tan asked about the processes to enhance data sharing and sensemaking by STRO.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Police had looked into these alerts, as I shared in my Ministerial Statement last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where possible offences are detected, STRO disseminates financial intelligence to law enforcement agencies or regulators for further investigations and appropriate actions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In response to Mr Tan and Mr Leong's queries, supervisory follow-ups and investigations had been conducted against the regulated entities and individuals relevant to the recent money laundering case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The amendments will allow STRO to develop richer financial intelligence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: STRO regularly engages gatekeepers and their regulators to discuss ways to enhance the quality of STRs filed and the efficiency of the processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The amendments will further enhance upstream detection by allowing regulators to access the STRs filed by their regulated entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is already the case for regulators, such as MAS, MinLaw and the Gambling Regulatory Authority.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The amendments do not change the existing process of how entities like the banks handle assets after filing an STR.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is also no obligation for filers to withhold transactions unless, of course, they have assessed the risk to be unacceptable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Likewise, any tipping off or disclosure of information relating to the filing of STRs continues to be an offence under section 57 of the CDSA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: STRO will continue to update its capabilities to keep pace with the evolving operational needs and share relevant intelligence with the community of regulators and gatekeepers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We agree with Mr Choo, Mr Ng, Mr Parekh, Mr Wee and Mr Yip on the importance of data safeguards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are strong legal safeguards and information security protocols within STRO to protect and prevent unauthorised access to all data received by STRO, including tax and trade data.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Only selected STRO personnel are authorised to request relevant tax or trade data from IRAS or Singapore Customs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are strictly prohibited from onward sharing of the data.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Furthermore, STRO can only share the results of its analyses of tax and trade data.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where law enforcement agencies need tax or trade data for investigation or prosecution, they have to separately request them from the data owner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is regulated under the legislation relevant to that data.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, I will touch on the amendments to section 56 of the CDSA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This would in turn facilitate confiscation of illicit monies and any subsequent restitution to victims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To clarify, the Prosecution would still have to prove the physical element of the offence, namely that there was transferring, converting, receiving, or acquiring of the property by the accused.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Only the need to prove, as a physical element of the offence, that the property is in fact the benefits of criminal conduct.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Prosecution would also have to prove the necessary fault element – that the person dealing with the monies knew, or had reasonable grounds to believe, that he was dealing with benefits of criminal conduct.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Other jurisdictions such as Hong Kong and Australia already have similar laws where there is no need to prove a direct link between the property and criminal conduct.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A few Members have questions on reasonableness, both what the Prosecution must do to show reasonable grounds and defendants can do to demonstrate reasonable doubt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members will appreciate that we are unable to provide examples of how a defendant might show reasonable doubt to counter the Prosecution’s assertion of reasonable grounds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Explicitly spelling this out may also unwittingly benefit criminals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such a determination would be made by the Courts based on the specifics of the case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are not matters unfamiliar to the Courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Proof of reasonableness is something that they deal with all the time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: An innocent person engaged in legitimate business should easily be able to show that the monies received were not benefits from criminal conduct and that he did not have the necessary fault element.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Legitimate businesses that do not break the laws in Singapore, therefore, need not worry about this amendment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Police will continue to raise awareness on the consequences of being unwittingly involved as money mules or in other criminal activities through advisories and public education campaigns.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On international cooperation, Singapore actively leverages MLA arrangements with bilateral counterparts and multilateral platforms, such as INTERPOL’s Global Rapid Intervention of Payments, Egmont Group and the Asset Recovery Interagency Network Asia Pacific, to trace, intercept and freeze criminal proceeds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will strengthen our partnership with international colleagues when there are good opportunities to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Government does not disclose the foreign jurisdictions from which we have received MLA requests, so as not to prejudice ongoing foreign criminal matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Goh, Mr Ng, Assoc Prof Razwana and Mr Wee also spoke on the introduction of the Third Schedule to CDSA, including its intent, impact on Police training and resourcing, and whether it would apply retrospectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This Schedule will be reviewed periodically, in tandem with evolving money laundering risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also regularly review the training and resourcing of law enforcement agencies to equip them with the capabilities to deal with these risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Foo, Mr Ng, Mr Saktiandi, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Wee and Mr Zhulkarnain sought clarifications on the processes involved in the early sale of seized property, including how law enforcement agencies assess whether a property is likely to depreciate, how the Court would determine whether the sale would be in the interests of justice, how the sale process would secure competitive prices, as well as the safeguards to ensure fairness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The underlying intent of these amendments is to preserve the value of seized or restrained properties, at reasonable costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Examples of assets which may be eligible to be sold under the amendments include vessels and vehicles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It might not be practical or desirable to set a standard threshold for the costs of maintenance or depreciation beyond which the seized assets will be sold.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The timeframe for assessment of the value of a seized property will depend on factors such as the estimated length of the investigations or court proceedings, and the expected rate and extent of depreciation of the value of the property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Agencies will generally look at open-source market value trends or seek expert opinion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mere fluctuations in valuation will not be sufficient for the Court to order an early sale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Seized properties will only be put up for early sale when there is no evidential value from the actual property that is necessary for investigations or court proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Before the application to the Court for the sale, law enforcement agencies will notify all known parties by delivering the notice personally through registered post or other prescribed modes of delivery under the CPC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If any person objects to the sale, he can raise this for the Court’s consideration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Furthermore, the Court can only order the sale of the property if it is satisfied that the costs of sale are, or are likely to be reasonable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are also established protocols on the conduct of the sale of seized property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In general, law enforcement agencies would follow established industry practice for the sale of particular properties, which can include public auctions or direct sale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Court will also have the flexibility to order the early sale of a property if the sale would be in the interests of justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In determining so, the Court may take into account various factors, such as the interests of the parties involved and whether there would be any injustice caused by the sale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Mr Ng's and Assoc Prof Razwana's questions on victim restitution process, this Bill does not change the current process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Victims with an interest in the property will be duly notified and the Court will assess what they are entitled to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is the latest we have, as the Police track the consolidated expenses on an annual basis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They also do not track the costs of asset depreciation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Seized assets will only be appropriated to the consolidated fund after the Court has ordered their disposal and they have been converted into cash.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Investigations are still ongoing for the remaining assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chia, Mr Tan, Mr Goh, Mr Saktiandi and Mr Zhulkarnain asked about the amendments to deal with seized properties linked to absconded persons, including their impact on foreign investors and the relevant safeguards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We thank Ms Foo’s for recognising that the amendments here, and I quote her, "strike at the heart of criminal networks and reinforce the principle that crime does not pay".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Law enforcement agencies are empowered to seize properties only in certain circumstances, as expressly provided for under sections 35 and 78 of the CPC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One such circumstance is when the law enforcement agency suspects that the properties are evidence of an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under the proposed amendments, the seized properties will continue to be dealt with in accordance with the CPC and subject to judicial oversight.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Interested persons can make their claims to the relevant Court and the Court will determine their entitlement to the properties and deal with it as appropriate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The mere fact that the seized property was a gift will not be sufficient, without other evidence, to prove a person’s entitlement to the property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will similarly apply to any donations by absconded persons that may have been seized.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There have been cases where persons, who were under investigation here but remained overseas, appointed counsel to apply for the release of their funds while investigations were ongoing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While there have been no successful claims by absconded persons thus far, the scenario of an absconded person remaining overseas to frustrate investigations while making a claim for his seized properties is a real possibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I reiterate these proposals are targeted at absconded persons, as well as properties linked to them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will now deal briefly with the other questions and suggestions which are outside the scope of this Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Leong asked about the adequacy of our sentencing regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This issue was dealt with during the Parliamentary Sitting last month and there is nothing more to add.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But allow me to reiterate the key points for the benefit of Members who may not have seen the written reply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, the maximum penalties for money laundering under the CDSA are comparable with the sentencing regime in other jurisdictions, such as Japan, Switzerland, New Zealand, Germany and France.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, the sentenced meted out for money laundering would depend on the nature of the offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The penalties for money laundering offences in the CDSA are comparable to those for other serious offences that are similar in nature, like cheating and forgery.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, the Courts independently considered the facts of the case to decide on the appropriate sentence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Generally, the Courts considered factors such as the length of the offending conduct, the culpability of the accused persons as well as the mitigating factors such as the accused person's plea of guilt and whether he has shown any remorse such as by voluntarily disgorging his illicit proceeds of crime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On Mr Goh, Assoc Prof Razwana and Mr Saktiandi’s questions about COSMIC, MAS will be providing updates in due course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Ms He's suggestion on the whistle-blowing programme, we will look into all leads that are worth investigating, whoever provides the information.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have to be practical because there are existing laws, and it is easier said than done to try and put everything together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What is most important is whether together our laws help us prevent, detect and enforce against money laundering effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And I believe the answer is that as we continue to update these laws through amendments such as those that are proposed today, we can keep our anti-money laundering regime robust and effective, whilst ensuring that our interest in promoting and strengthening our financial ecosystem is not compromised.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Earlier in my speech, I talked about STRs and I noted that in a previous reply by the Minister for Home Affairs, he had indicated that out of the STRs filed, 20% of them led to or assisted in the investigations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I wanted her comment on whether she finds that this percentage of 20% indicates that the quality of STRs still needs beefing up or is this percentage acceptable for some other reason?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a very interesting question and I think it is a reminder to us not to take any single number on its own and forget the context.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is the process that is still ongoing, and I think because the landscape for money laundering will change very quickly, what may look like very obvious signs of financial crime today will be superseded by new types of behaviour that deserve greater attention.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is, I think, the greater emphasis of where our efforts need to be.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Speaker, I have three questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First, she said there is no limit for the casinos to accept cash.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, can the Minister confirm that the casinos are actually allowed to take in more than a million dollars in cash in one go?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And, if possible, can we know what is the maximum amount of cash that our casinos have accepted?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second question is, while she said that the 13 months and 17 months sentencing given to the offenders are in line with international standards, can I ask whether, in the IMC review, will we be demonstrating our resolve further to look at this sentencing regime?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Is it part of the review that the IMC will do?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And my last question is, can the Minister update us what are the actions taken against all the institutions that are involved in this $3 billion money laundering case?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He asked specifically about what casinos may have received in terms of cash proceeds from their customers and from their patrons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, respectfully, I would ask the Member to file a PQ if it is something that he is very interested in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I believe his third question is also in terms of the actions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They do not relate directly to this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member did talk about sentencing and I think I have responded to it in my round-up speech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member himself has referred to Minister Shanmugam's reply to the Member at the Sitting in May.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What the Courts decide to mete out by way of the sentence itself is something for the Court to decide.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I have explained earlier what are the factors that the Courts look into.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think one thing that we need to keep in mind is that, ultimately, the Courts must consider what crime was committed within our jurisdiction.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The sums may be very large, but what was the activity in Singapore that constituted the crime?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is something we have to keep in mind.
